claims.text: High-entropy alloys exhibit superior wear-corrosion resistance.
Multicomponent oxide films can rapidly re-form after mechanical damage.
Rapid re-formation of multicomponent oxide films maintains a protective barrier and thereby improves wear-corrosion resistance.
The alloys under consideration initially possess a well-developed, homogeneous passive oxide layer.
The composition and structural integrity of the surface oxide film govern wear-corrosion behavior.
The alloy's complex elemental makeup promotes rapid repassivation.
Mechanical wear removes portions of the protective oxide layer.
After oxide removal, exposed alloying elements quickly form a new, stable oxide.
Rapid formation of a new stable oxide mitigates subsequent corrosive attack.
High-entropy configurations optimized for repassivation will recover their passive films faster than a slower-repassivating baseline alloy.
Faster passive-film recovery will produce lower total material loss than in the baseline alloy.
The protective benefit should occur when film removal is partial and repassivation kinetics remain effective.
The protective mechanism may fail under extreme wear that continually exposes the substrate.
The protective mechanism may fail in environments that inhibit repassivation.
The quantitative relationship among alloy composition, repassivation rate, and overall wear-corrosion resistance may vary among high-entropy alloy systems.
